16.01.title: Springs to stiffness matrices
16.01.html:
The finite element method (FEM) analyses everything from bike frames to dams. Its core idea fits in a chain of springs: break a structure into simple pieces (elements), write the force-displacement law of one piece as a small matrix, and add all the pieces into one big system. Phase 16 builds that machinery from scratch, one step at a time, until it handles 2D and 3D solids, vibration and nonlinearity.

One spring, one matrix

A spring of stiffness k connects node i to node j. The force it exerts depends only on the stretch uj​−ui​. The forces on its two ends are

[fi​fj​​]=k[1−1​−11​][ui​uj​​].

That 2 × 2 matrix is the element stiffness matrix. It is symmetric, and it is singular: moving both ends together (ui​=uj​) produces no force. That is a rigid-body mode.

Assembly

At each node, the external force must balance the sum of the spring forces from every element attached to it. So the global system Ku=F is built by adding each element matrix into the rows and columns of its two nodes. This assembly step is the same for every element type in this phase; only the element matrix changes.

The assembled K is still singular, because the whole chain can slide. Supports fix that: a node with prescribed zero displacement has its row and column removed, the reduced system is solved, and the removed rows then give the reaction forces, R=Ku−F.

For springs in a chain, the result must match the series formula 1/keq​=∑1/ke​, and every spring carries the same force.

Worked exampleA four-spring chain

Springs of 200, 100, 400 and 250 N/mm in a chain, fixed at node 0, pulled with 1 kN at node 4.

  1. Assembly gives a 5 × 5 tridiagonal matrix. Row 2, for example, is [0,−100,500,−400,0]: node 2 touches the 100 and the 400 N/mm springs.
  2. Remove node 0 and solve: displacements 0, 5, 15, 17.5 and 21.5 mm.
  3. Tip stiffness 1000/21.5=46.512 N/mm. The series formula gives 1/(1/200+1/100+1/400+1/250)=46.512 N/mm.
  4. Reaction at node 0: −1000 N. Each spring carries exactly 1000 N, for example 100⋅(15−5)=1000 N.
  5. With both ends fixed and loads of +300 N at node 1 and −200 N at node 3, the reactions are −193.02 N and +93.02 N; they sum to −100 N, balancing the net applied +100 N.

16.02.title: Direct stiffness method for trusses
16.02.html:
A truss is a set of bars joined by pins, like a footbridge or the frame of a crane. Each bar is just a spring along its own axis, with k=EA/L. The only new ingredient compared with the spring chain is direction: a bar at an angle pushes its end nodes both horizontally and vertically. With that one change, the same assembly solves any 2D truss.

A bar in global axes

Let a bar run from node i to node j at angle θ, with c=cosθ, s=sinθ. Its stretch is the relative displacement projected on its axis, δ=c(uj​−ui​)+s(vj​−vi​). Its force N=(EA/L)δ acts along the axis on both nodes. Written for the four displacements [ui​,vi​,uj​,vj​]:

ke​=LEA​​c2cs−c2−cs​css2−cs−s2​−c2−csc2cs​−cs−s2css2​​=LEA​ttT,t=[c,s,−c,−s]T.

This is the spring matrix rotated into global axes. Assembly puts each ke​ into the rows and columns of its four degrees of freedom; supports remove fixed degrees of freedom; solve; and each bar’s force follows from its end displacements: N=(EA/L)[c(uj​−ui​)+s(vj​−vi​)], tension positive.

The check: statics

If a truss has exactly as many unknowns (bar forces plus reactions) as joint equilibrium equations, m+r=2n, it is statically determinate: the forces follow from equilibrium alone, whatever the stiffness. The method of joints writes ∑Fx​=0 and ∑Fy​=0 at every joint and solves them as one linear system. For a determinate truss, the stiffness method must give exactly the same bar forces. For an indeterminate truss (extra bars), only the stiffness method works, because the force split then depends on the stiffnesses.

Worked exampleA Pratt footbridge truss

Four panels of 3 m, 2.5 m deep. Steel bars with EA=210 GPa⋅1200 mm2. Pin at the left, roller at the right; deck loads of 20, 30 and 20 kN at the three inner bottom joints. Eight joints, 13 bars and 3 reactions: 13+3=16=2⋅8, so it is determinate.

  1. Reactions 35 kN at each support (by symmetry).
  2. End diagonals: length 32+2.52​=3.905 m, so the force is 35⋅3.905/2.5=54.67 kN in compression. The bottom chord carries its horizontal component, 35⋅3/2.5=42.0 kN in tension.
  3. Top chord at mid-span: moment 35⋅6−20⋅3=150 kN·m over a depth of 2.5 m gives 60.0 kN compression.
  4. The FEM solver and the method of joints agree on all 13 bar forces and the 3 reactions to within 10−6 N. The middle vertical carries nothing; the inner diagonals carry 23.43 kN in tension.
  5. Mid-span deflection 4.805 mm, about span/2500. Only the stiffness method gives this.
